claim: Successful episodic memory involves dynamic increases in activity across distributed hippocampal networks, including the posterior-medial (PMN) and the anterior-temporal (ATN) networks.
source: Successful episodic memory involves dynamic increases in activity across distributed hippocampal networks, including the posterior-medial (PMN) and the anterior-temporal (ATN) networks.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about hippocampal network function in memory, as reflected in the manuscript's introduction and background.

claim: PMN-targeted stimulation significantly increased connectivity during autobiographical retrieval versus rest within the PMN.
source: PMN-targeted stimulation significantly increased connectivity during autobiographical retrieval versus rest within the PMN.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in the results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The effect of PMN-targeted stimulation on connectivity was not observed in the ATN.
source: This effect was not observed in the ATN, or in either network following control stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no significant three-way interaction in the ATN (T(89)=1.48, p=0.14).

claim: Task-dependent increases in connectivity within the medial temporal lobe predicted improved performance of a separate episodic memory test.
source: Task-dependent increases in connectivity within the medial temporal lobe predicted improved performance of a separate episodic memory test.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing correlation between connectivity changes and memory performance (Figure 5).

claim: It is possible to enhance the task-dependent regulation of hippocampal network connectivity that supports memory processing using noninvasive stimulation.
source: It is therefore possible to enhance the task-dependent regulation of hippocampal network connectivity that supports memory processing using noninvasive stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental findings demonstrating that PMN-targeted stimulation increased task-dependent connectivity.

claim: Episodic memory depends on the hippocampus.
source: Episodic memory depends on the hippocampus (Scoville and Milner, 1957; Squire, 1992) as well as on the distributed set of regions that form a hippocampal-cortical network (Buckner et al., 2008; Rugg and Vilberg, 2013; Eichenbaum, 2000; Ranganath et al., 2005; Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational studies in the field.

claim: The hippocampal-cortical network comprises distinct anterior-temporal and posterior-medial components.
source: as well as on the distributed set of regions that form a hippocampal-cortical network (Buckner et al., 2008; Rugg and Vilberg, 2013; Eichenbaum, 2000; Ranganath et al., 2005; Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012) comprising distinct anterior-temporal and posterior-medial components (Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012; Libby et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies characterizing hippocampal network organization.

claim: Invasive stimulation of the hippocampus or its direct mesial-temporal afferents has primarily been associated with memory disruption.
source: Invasive stimulation of the hippocampus or its direct mesial-temporal afferents has primarily been associated with memory disruption (Jacobs et al., 2016; Goyal et al., 2018; Kucewicz et al., 2018a; Mohan, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies showing disruptive effects of invasive hippocampal stimulation.

claim: Hippocampal network regions can serve as a target for memory improvement.
source: However, hippocampal network regions can serve as a target for memory improvement (Mohan, 2019; Ezzyat et al., 2018; Kucewicz et al., 2018b; Miller et al., 2015; Shirvalkar et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating memory improvement through stimulation of hippocampal network regions.

claim: Noninvasive transcranial electromagnetic stimulation (TMS) targeting cortical PMN locations has been shown to improve memory.
source: Noninvasive transcranial electromagnetic stimulation (TMS) targeting cortical PMN locations has been shown to improve memory (Tambini et al., 2018; Hermiller et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2014; Nilakantan et al., 2019; Nilakantan et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies showing memory improvement from PMN-targeted TMS.

claim: PMN-targeted TMS alters hippocampal-cortical network fMRI activity.
source: and alter hippocampal-cortical network fMRI activity (Tambini et al., 2018; Hermiller et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2014; Nilakantan et al., 2019), especially within the PMN (Kim et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2014; Nilakantan et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating fMRI activity changes following PMN-targeted TMS.

claim: PMN-targeted stimulation increases connectivity among PMN regions.
source: Because PMN-targeted stimulation increases connectivity among PMN regions and relatively low hippocampal-cortical network connectivity is associated with poor episodic memory (Beason-Held, 2011; Grady et al., 2006; Lustig et al., 2003; Damoiseaux et al., 2008; Froudist-Walsh et al., 2018; Henson et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from cited studies and the experimental context.

claim: Relatively low hippocampal-cortical network connectivity is associated with poor episodic memory.
source: and relatively low hippocampal-cortical network connectivity is associated with poor episodic memory (Beason-Held, 2011; Grady et al., 2006; Lustig et al., 2003; Damoiseaux et al., 2008; Froudist-Walsh et al., 2018; Henson et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies linking low connectivity with poor memory.

claim: Successful memory typically relies on dynamic reconfiguration of fMRI connectivity within the PMN and ATN in response to memory demands.
source: However, successful memory typically relies on dynamic reconfiguration of fMRI connectivity within the PMN and ATN in response to memory demands (Warren et al., 2018; Gratton et al., 2016; Kim and Voss, 2019; Westphal et al., 2017; King et al., 2015; Geib et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating task-dependent connectivity changes during memory processing.

claim: Effective memory encoding and retrieval is associated with location-specific and task-dependent increases of stimulus-evoked fMRI activity within the hippocampal-cortical network.
source: For instance, effective memory encoding and retrieval is associated with location-specific and task-dependent increases of stimulus-evoked fMRI activity within the network (Paller and Wagner, 2002; Paller, 1997; Wagner et al., 1998; Buckner et al., 2001; Kirchhoff et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing task-dependent activity increases during memory processing.

claim: Better memory is predicted by fMRI connectivity related to specific memory processes, such as recollection.
source: Correspondingly, better memory is predicted by fMRI connectivity related to specific memory processes, such as recollection (Kim and Voss, 2019; King et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies linking specific connectivity patterns with memory performance.

claim: Theta-gamma synchrony in the hippocampus is observed during memory processing in rodents.
source: In rodents, theta-gamma synchrony in the hippocampus is observed during memory processing, indicating connectivity changes modulated by memory demands (Shirvalkar et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a rodent study demonstrating theta-gamma synchrony during memory tasks.

claim: Pharmacological disruption of hippocampal theta-gamma synchrony and memory can be rescued by theta-burst stimulation of the fornix.
source: Pharmacological disruption of hippocampal theta-gamma synchrony and memory can be rescued by theta-burst stimulation of the fornix, indicating that this marker of connectivity is critical for memory (Shirvalkar et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study showing rescue of memory deficits through fornix stimulation.

claim: Amnestic states caused by hippocampal lesions are associated with reduced hippocampal-cortical connectivity.
source: Furthermore, amnestic states, such as those caused by hippocampal lesions, are associated not only with reduced hippocampal-cortical connectivity, but also with increased connectivity between the hippocampal network and other networks (Froudist-Walsh et al., 2018; Henson et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies characterizing connectivity changes in amnesia.

claim: Amnestic states are associated with increased connectivity between the hippocampal network and other networks.
source: Furthermore, amnestic states, such as those caused by hippocampal lesions, are associated not only with reduced hippocampal-cortical connectivity, but also with increased connectivity between the hippocampal network and other networks (Froudist-Walsh et al., 2018; Henson et al., 2016), suggesting that nonspecific increases in connectivity can be problematic.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing aberrant connectivity patterns in amnesia.

claim: Thirty-two adults participated in the experiment (22 females, mean age = 25.6 years, range = 18–34).
source: Thirty-two adults participated in the experiment (22 females, mean age = 25.6 years, range = 18–34).
evidence: This claim describes the participant demographics as reported in the methods section.

claim: Data from two additional participants were collected but discarded due to excessive motion.
source: Data from two additional participants were collected but discarded due to excessive motion (see below).
evidence: This claim describes data exclusion criteria applied in the study.

claim: One group of participants (n = 16) received multi-session, high-frequency TMS targeting the PMN via parietal cortex.
source: One group of participants (n = 16) received multi-session, high-frequency TMS targeting the PMN via parietal cortex, which is a robust component of the PMN (Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012; Libby et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design and is supported by the study protocol.

claim: Parietal cortex is a robust component of the PMN.
source: which is a robust component of the PMN (Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012; Libby et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies characterizing the PMN.

claim: A separate control group (n = 16) received the same TMS regimen targeting a control prefrontal cortex (PFC) location that is not robustly part of the PMN.
source: A separate control group (n = 16) received the same TMS regimen targeting a control prefrontal cortex (PFC) location that is not robustly part of the PMN.
evidence: This claim describes the control condition in the experimental design.

claim: Each group received site-specific sham-control stimulation, delivered at a subthreshold intensity which should not influence brain function.
source: Each group also received site-specific sham-control stimulation, delivered at a subthreshold intensity which should not influence brain function, administered in counterbalanced order with real stimulation (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim describes the sham control condition and is based on the assumption that subthreshold stimulation does not affect brain function.

claim: The memory retrieval task involved extended periods of autobiographical memory retrieval.
source: The memory retrieval task involved extended periods of autobiographical memory retrieval, which has been shown to cause robust hippocampal-cortical network connectivity changes primarily in PMN regions compared to the resting state (Warren et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim describes the task design and is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Autobiographical memory retrieval causes robust hippocampal-cortical network connectivity changes primarily in PMN regions compared to the resting state.
source: which has been shown to cause robust hippocampal-cortical network connectivity changes primarily in PMN regions compared to the resting state (Warren et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study demonstrating connectivity changes during autobiographical retrieval.

claim: Stimulation effects on PMN interconnectivity were greater during retrieval versus rest following PMN-targeted stimulation relative to PFC-targeted stimulation (3-way interaction: T(89)=2.80, p=0.006).
source: Indeed, stimulation effects on PMN interconnectivity were greater during retrieval versus rest following PMN-targeted stimulation relative to PFC-targeted stimulation (3-way interaction: T(89)=2.80, p=0.006) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Task-sensitive relative interconnectivity increase for PMN-targeted versus PFC-targeted stimulation was not found for the ATN (3-way interaction: T(89)=1.48, p=0.14).
source: This task-sensitive relative interconnectivity increase for PMN-targeted versus PFC-targeted stimulation was not found for the ATN (3-way interaction: T(89)=1.48, p=0.14) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant effect in the ATN.

claim: PMN-targeted stimulation, relative to sham, significantly increased task-dependent connectivity during retrieval versus rest in the PMN (T(45)=2.02, p=0.049).
source: As shown in Figure 2A, PMN-targeted stimulation, relative to sham, significantly increased task-dependent connectivity during retrieval versus rest (interaction of stimulation condition and task) in the PMN (T(45)=2.02, p=0.049)
evidence: This claim is directly supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: PMN-targeted stimulation led to a numeric but non-significant increase in task-dependent connectivity in the ATN (T(45)=0.60, p=0.55).
source: but led to a numeric but non-significant increase in the ATN (T(45)=0.60, p=0.55).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant effect in the ATN.

claim: Task-dependent connectivity decreased non-significantly in both networks for the group of subjects receiving PFC-targeted stimulation (PMN: T(45)=-1.60, p=0.12; ATN: T(45)=-1.06, p=0.29).
source: In contrast, task-dependent connectivity decreased non-significantly in both networks for the group of subjects receiving PFC-targeted stimulation (PMN: T(45)=-1.60, p=0.12; ATN: T(45)=-1.06, p=0.29).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the PFC-targeted stimulation group.

claim: The pairwise connections showing significantly greater task-dependent stimulation effects during retrieval following PMN-targeted stimulation included higher-order visual regions of the PMN, especially precuneus and lingual gyrus, with the hippocampus.
source: The pairwise connections showing significantly greater task-dependent stimulation effects during retrieval following PMN-targeted stimulation following correction for multiple comparisons (Figure 2B) included higher-order visual regions of the PMN, especially precuneus and lingual gyrus, with the hippocampus.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of pairwise connectivity data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Hippocampal connectivity with precuneus and lingual gyrus has been particularly implicated in episodic recollection.
source: Notably, hippocampal connectivity with these regions has been particularly implicated in episodic recollection (Rugg and Vilberg, 2013; King et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies linking these connectivity patterns with recollection.

claim: Within the PMN, hippocampus, precuneus, and lingual gyrus exhibited significant increases in task-dependent connectivity with the rest of the network.
source: Within the PMN, the same regions showing pairwise task-dependent connectivity increases (hippocampus, precuenus, and lingual gyrus) also exhibited significant increases in task-dependent connectivity with the rest of the network, after correcting for multiple comparisons (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of region-to-network connectivity shown in Figure 2C.

claim: No ATN regions showed significant increases in task-dependent connectivity with the rest of the network.
source: No ATN regions showed these effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by the absence of significant effects in the ATN analysis.

claim: There was a main effect of task in the PMN and the broader hippocampal-cortical network with greater connectivity during the retrieval task than during rest.
source: There was a main effect of task in the PMN and the broader hippocampal-cortical network as well as regions typically associated with autobiographical memory, with greater connectivity during the retrieval task than during rest (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-brain analysis showing task effects on connectivity.

claim: The main effect of task on connectivity replicates previous findings using this analysis method and retrieval task.
source: This replicates our previous findings using this analysis method and retrieval task, and is consistent with many findings of fMRI connectivity increases due to similar memory retrieval tasks (Svoboda et al., 2006; Bellana et al., 2017; McCormick et al., 2015; Rabin et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous studies showing similar task effects.

claim: There were many regions that exhibited significantly greater stimulation effects on whole-brain connectivity during retrieval versus rest following PMN-targeted stimulation relative to PFC-targeted control stimulation.
source: Consistent with the targeted network analysis, there were many regions that exhibited significantly greater stimulation effects on whole-brain connectivity during retrieval versus rest following PMN-targeted stimulation relative to PFC-targeted control stimulation (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-brain analysis results shown in Figure 3.

claim: For the PMN-targeted stimulation group, there was significant interaction of stimulation by task in many regions particularly within the PMN.
source: For the PMN-targeted stimulation group, there was significant interaction of stimulation by task in many regions particularly within the PMN (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of the PMN-targeted stimulation group shown in Figure 4A.

claim: All but one area showed relatively greater connectivity for stimulation relative to sham during retrieval compared to rest in the PMN-targeted stimulation group.
source: All but one area showed relatively greater connectivity for stimulation relative to sham during retrieval compared to rest, thereby demonstrating the hypothesized task-dependent increase in fMRI connectivity due to stimulation independently in the group of subjects receiving PMN-targeted stimulation (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of connectivity direction shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The majority of regions (93.5%) demonstrating the interaction effect overlapped with the network that was sensitive to autobiographical retrieval.
source: The majority of regions (93.5%) demonstrating this interaction effect overlapped with the network that was sensitive to autobiographical retrieval (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), indicating that task-dependent connectivity changes due to stimulation occurred for regions that contribute to memory retrieval.
evidence: This claim is supported by spatial overlap analysis between stimulation effects and task-sensitive regions.

claim: 61% of regions demonstrating the interaction effect were within a priori defined hippocampal-cortical network locations (8 PMN, 2 ATN, and 1 DMN).
source: Furthermore, 61% of regions demonstrating the interaction effect were within a priori defined hippocampal-cortical network locations (8 PMN, 2 ATN, and 1 DMN, see Materials and methods), especially in the PMN
evidence: This claim is supported by categorization of regions showing stimulation effects.

claim: PFC-targeted control stimulation caused a nearly opposite pattern of fMRI connectivity change relative to PMN-targeted stimulation.
source: PFC-targeted control stimulation caused a nearly opposite pattern of fMRI connectivity change relative to PMN-targeted stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of connectivity patterns between the two stimulation groups.

claim: All regions showed the opposite direction of connectivity changes relative to PMN-targeted stimulation, with greater connectivity during rest than during retrieval following PFC-targeted stimulation relative to sham.
source: However, all regions showed the opposite direction of connectivity changes relative to PMN-targeted stimulation, with greater connectivity during rest than during retrieval following PFC-targeted stimulation relative to sham (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of connectivity direction in the PFC-targeted group shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The area of prefrontal cortex stimulated in the control condition does not overlap with either the PMN or the ATN.
source: Notably, the area of prefrontal cortex stimulated in the control condition does not overlap with either the PMN or the ATN and participates in a variety of non-memory cognitive operations such as attention and maintenance of external awareness (Van Calster et al., 2017; Chou et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical characterization and citations to studies of prefrontal cortex function.

claim: Stimulation of the control location may have caused a relative increase in attention and external awareness operations during rest and/or a disruption of memory-related processing during the retrieval task.
source: Stimulation of the control location may thus have caused a relative increase in these operations during rest and/or a disruption of memory-related processing during the retrieval task.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the observed connectivity patterns and known functions of the stimulated region.

claim: PMN-targeted stimulation produced memory task-dependent increases in connectivity in 31 PMN regions and only 5 ATN regions.
source: As in the targeted analysis of effects on PMN and ATN (Figure 2), PMN-targeted stimulation produced memory task-dependent increases in connectivity in 31 PMN regions and only 5 ATN regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by categorization of regions showing stimulation effects.

claim: PFC-targeted stimulation produced memory task-dependent decreases in an evenly distributed set of PMN and ATN regions (12 PMN regions, 13 ATN regions).
source: In contrast, PFC-targeted stimulation produced memory task-dependent decreases in an evenly distributed set of PMN and ATN regions (12 PMN regions, 13 ATN regions).
evidence: This claim is supported by categorization of regions showing effects of PFC-targeted stimulation.

claim: There was a significant difference in the relative distribution of task-dependent effects on PMN versus ATN regions in the PMN-targeted relative to PFC-targeted stimulation conditions (Yates-corrected X2(1)=8.56, p=0.003).
source: There was a significant difference in the relative distribution of task-dependent effects (irrespective of directionality) on PMN versus ATN regions in the PMN-targeted relative to PFC-targeted stimulation conditions (Yates-corrected X2(1)=8.56, p=0.003).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of regional distributions between stimulation conditions.

claim: The relatively selective effects of stimulation on PMN were consistent across the targeted analysis of PMN and ATN regions of interest and the whole-brain analyses.
source: Thus, the relatively selective effects of stimulation on PMN were consistent across the targeted analysis of PMN and ATN regions of interest and the whole-brain analyses.
evidence: This claim is supported by convergence of findings across different analysis approaches.

claim: Context recollection is more heavily dependent on the PMN than item recognition.
source: Because context recollection is more heavily dependent on the PMN than item recognition (Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012; Libby et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies characterizing functional distinctions between PMN and ATN.

claim: PMN-targeted stimulation would improve context recollection selectively.
source: and based on our previous findings (Kim et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2014; Nilakantan et al., 2019; Nilakantan et al., 2017), we predicted that PMN-targeted stimulation would improve context recollection selectively (Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012).
evidence: This claim represents a hypothesis based on previous findings and theoretical considerations.

claim: There were no baseline differences in memory performance before stimulation was delivered (pre-stimulation vs pre-sham: T(31)=-1.23, p=0.23).
source: Considering both stimulation groups, there were no baseline differences in memory performance before stimulation was delivered (pre-stimulation vs pre-sham: T(31)=-1.23, p=0.23).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of baseline memory performance.

claim: PMN-targeted stimulation improved context recollection (post-stimulation vs post-sham: T(15)=1.93, p=0.036).
source: Consistent with the previously reported results in 30 of the 32 subjects analyzed here (Kim et al., 2018), PMN-targeted stimulation improved context recollection (post-stimulation vs post-sham: T(15)=1.93, p=0.036)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of memory performance data.

claim: PFC-targeted control stimulation did not improve context recollection (post-stimulation vs post-sham: T(15)=-0.09, p=0.46).
source: whereas PFC-targeted control stimulation did not (post-stimulation vs post-sham: T(15)=-0.09, p=0.46)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant effect of PFC-targeted stimulation on context recollection.

claim: There was significantly greater improvement in context recollection for PMN-targeted stimulation relative to PFC-targeted stimulation (T(15)=1.88, p=0.04).
source: with significantly greater improvement for PMN-targeted stimulation relative to PFC-targeted stimulation (T(15)=1.88, p=0.04).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of memory improvement between stimulation groups.

claim: Stimulation had no effect on item recognition for either stimulation location (PMN-targeted: T(15)=0.94, p=0.36; PFC-targeted: T(15)=-1.34, p=0.20).
source: Stimulation had no effect on item recognition for either stimulation location (PMN-targeted: T(15)=0.94, p=0.36; PFC-targeted: T(15)=-1.34, p=0.20).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant effects on item recognition.

claim: The amount that PMN-targeted stimulation caused task-dependent increases in connectivity for retrieval versus rest was associated with greater improvement in context recollection memory (robust regression F(15) = 6.64, r2 = 0.12, p=0.022).
source: The amount that PMN-targeted stimulation caused task-dependent increases in connectivity for retrieval versus rest was associated with greater improvement in context recollection memory (robust regression F(15) = 6.64, r2 = 0.12, p=0.022).
evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis relating connectivity changes to memory improvement.

claim: For PFC-targeted stimulation, relative increases in connectivity during retrieval than during rest predicted relative improvement in source recollection (robust regression F(15)=11.14, r2 = 0.16, p=0.005).
source: That is, relative increases in connectivity during retrieval than during rest predicted relative improvement in source recollection (robust regression F(15)=11.14, r2 = 0.16, p=0.005).
evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis in the PFC-targeted stimulation group.

claim: Irrespective of stimulation condition, the degree to which stimulation increased task-dependent connectivity during retrieval compared to rest predicted the amount of context recollection improvement (F(31) = 6.71, r2 = 0.12, p=0.01).
source: Based on the similarity of these effects, we pooled connectivity values across the two regions of interest and found that, irrespective of stimulation condition, the degree to which stimulation increased task-dependent connectivity during retrieval compared to rest predicted the amount of context recollection improvement (F(31) = 6.71, r2 = 0.12, p=0.01) (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis pooling data across both stimulation groups.

claim: Memory task-dependent connectivity increases for the left medial temporal lobe is a robust indicator of episodic memory improvement due to stimulation.
source: Thus, memory task-dependent connectivity increases for the left medial temporal lobe is a robust indicator of episodic memory improvement due to stimulation.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the correlation between task-dependent connectivity and memory improvement.

claim: These findings demonstrate memory task-dependent increases in the expression of fMRI connectivity changes caused by PMN-targeted stimulation.
source: These findings demonstrate memory task-dependent increases in the expression of fMRI connectivity changes caused by PMN-targeted stimulation.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main finding supported by the experimental data.

claim: Task-dependent connectivity effects were selective to a priori defined regions of the PMN relative to the ATN.
source: These effects were selective to a priori defined regions of the PMN relative to the ATN, which was confirmed via exploratory whole-brain analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by both targeted and whole-brain analyses showing PMN selectivity.

claim: Task-dependent connectivity increases were specific to the PMN-targeted stimulation condition, relative to PFC-targeted control stimulation.
source: Task-dependent connectivity increases in these regions were also specific to the PMN-targeted stimulation condition, relative to PFC-targeted control stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison between stimulation conditions.

claim: Retrieval-related connectivity increases in left medial temporal cortex and hippocampus due to stimulation predicted context recollection improvement measured in a separate task.
source: Furthermore, retrieval-related connectivity increases in left medial temporal cortex and hippocampus due to stimulation predicted context recollection improvement measured in a separate task.
evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis relating connectivity to memory performance.

claim: Enhancing hippocampal connectivity during memory processing is functionally critical and is achievable via noninvasive stimulation.
source: Thus, enhancing hippocampal connectivity during memory processing is functionally critical and is achievable via noninvasive stimulation.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the experimental findings showing connectivity enhancement and its relationship to memory.

claim: Task-dependent effects were measured ~ 24 hr after stimulation.
source: Furthermore, these task-dependent effects were measured ~ 24 hr after stimulation, indicating that stimulation led to upregulation of connectivity during a subsequent memory task administered long after, and without any specific relationship to, stimulation delivery.
evidence: This claim describes the timing of measurements in the experimental design.

claim: Stimulation led to upregulation of connectivity during a subsequent memory task administered long after, and without any specific relationship to, stimulation delivery.
source: indicating that stimulation led to upregulation of connectivity during a subsequent memory task administered long after, and without any specific relationship to, stimulation delivery.
evidence: This claim is an inference about the lasting effects of stimulation based on the timing of measurements.

claim: The PMN and ATN are functionally distinct components of the larger hippocampal-cortical network.
source: The PMN and ATN are functionally distinct components of the larger hippocampal-cortical network and are thought to differentially support memory processing related to context recollection versus item recognition, respectively (Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012; Libby et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies characterizing functional distinctions between PMN and ATN.

claim: The PMN and ATN differentially support memory processing related to context recollection versus item recognition, respectively.
source: and are thought to differentially support memory processing related to context recollection versus item recognition, respectively (Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012; Libby et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies characterizing functional roles of PMN and ATN.

claim: Increased connectivity due to stimulation was selective for PMN regions and for the autobiographical memory retrieval task.
source: Here, we report that increased connectivity due to stimulation was selective for PMN regions and for the autobiographical memory retrieval task.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main finding of selectivity for PMN and task.

claim: This selectivity is consistent with the role of the PMN in autobiographical memory retrieval.
source: This selectivity is consistent with the role of the PMN in autobiographical memory retrieval (Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012)
evidence: This claim relates the findings to established knowledge about PMN function, supported by citation.

claim: The selectivity of stimulation effects is consistent with the stimulation location, which was within the PMN.
source: as well as with the stimulation location, which was within the PMN (Libby et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim relates the findings to the experimental design, supported by citation characterizing the PMN.

claim: These findings are consonant with previous reports that the same stimulation protocol increased stimulus-evoked activity during the encoding of item-context pairings selectively within the PMN.
source: These findings are consonant with our previous report that the same stimulation protocol increased stimulus-evoked activity during the encoding of item-context pairings selectively within the PMN (Kim et al., 2018; Nilakantan et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim relates current findings to previous studies using the same stimulation protocol.

claim: The findings further support hypothesized functional distinctions of the PMN and ATN.
source: and further supports hypothesized functional distinctions of the PMN and ATN.
evidence: This claim is an inference about theoretical implications of the findings.

claim: Connectivity changes due to stimulation were measured during a memory retrieval task (autobiographical retrieval task) versus rest, yet they predicted the effects of stimulation on memory ability measured using an independent item/source episodic memory test.
source: Connectivity changes due to stimulation were measured during a memory retrieval task (autobiographical retrieval task) versus rest, yet they predicted the effects of stimulation on memory ability measured using an independent item/source episodic memory test.
evidence: This claim describes the relationship between connectivity measures and memory performance across different tasks.

claim: Although autobiographical retrieval and episodic memory are superficially distinct, there is accumulating evidence that they are supported by similar cognitive operations and brain regions.
source: Although autobiographical retrieval and episodic memory are superficially distinct, there is accumulating evidence that they are supported by similar cognitive operations and brain regions (McCormick et al., 2015; Andrews-Hanna et al., 2014; Burianova et al., 2010; Daselaar et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing overlap between autobiographical and episodic memory systems.

claim: The findings of a relationship of stimulation effects on connectivity during autobiographical retrieval with episodic memory performance underscores the similarity between autobiographical retrieval and episodic memory.
source: Our findings of a relationship of stimulation effects on connectivity during autobiographical retrieval with episodic memory performance underscores this similarity.
evidence: This claim is an inference about the implications of the correlation between connectivity and memory performance.

claim: PMN-targeted stimulation parameters used in this study improve a variety of episodic memory tasks of different formats, including face-word paired associates, item-scene paired associates, item-location associations, and precise spatial recall.
source: Indeed, we have previously found that the PMN-targeted stimulation parameters used here improve a variety of episodic memory tasks of different formats, including face-word paired associates (Wang et al., 2014), item-scene paired associates (Kim et al., 2018; Nilakantan et al., 2019), item-location associations (Kim et al., 2018; Nilakantan et al., 2019), and precise spatial recall (Nilakantan et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies showing memory improvements across various tasks.

claim: The current findings emphasize that stimulation targeting the PMN improves a variety of memory measures.
source: Although we did not assess stimulation effects on the success of autobiographical memory retrieval, the current findings emphasize that stimulation targeting the PMN improves a variety of memory measures.
evidence: This claim is an inference about the generalizability of stimulation effects based on current and previous findings.

claim: Memory tasks including paired associate, spatial recall, episodic, and autobiographical memory have all been associated with the PMN.
source: Though these memory tasks are typically considered distinct (paired associate versus spatial recall, episodic versus autobiographical), they all have been associated with the PMN (Buckner et al., 2008; Svoboda et al., 2006; McCormick et al., 2015; Andrews-Hanna et al., 2014; Burianova et al., 2010; Daselaar et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies linking various memory tasks to the PMN.

claim: Various memory tasks likely all respond to PMN-targeted stimulation because they are associated with the PMN.
source: and therefore all likely respond to PMN-targeted stimulation.
evidence: This claim is an inference about why different memory tasks respond to PMN-targeted stimulation.

claim: Resting-state fMRI connectivity has proven useful in characterizing the effects of stimulation on brain network function, including to understand memory improvements due to stimulation.
source: Although resting-state fMRI connectivity has proven useful in characterizing the effects of stimulation on brain network function, including to understand memory improvements due to stimulation (Tambini et al., 2018; Hermiller et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2014; Kim and Voss, 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies using resting-state fMRI to assess stimulation effects.

claim: The current findings highlight one of the many limitations of resting-state fMRI for characterizing stimulation effects.
source: the current findings highlight one of the many limitations of resting-state fMRI for this purpose.
evidence: This claim is an inference about the limitations of resting-state fMRI based on the current findings.

claim: Relationships between resting-state connectivity and network function are not well specified.
source: That is, relationships between resting-state connectivity and network function are not well specified.
evidence: This claim reflects a general limitation in the field regarding interpretation of resting-state connectivity.

claim: There was strong modulation of the effects of stimulation on connectivity based on whether it was measured during a memory retrieval task versus during rest.
source: Here, there was strong modulation of the effects of stimulation on connectivity based on whether it was measured during a memory retrieval task versus during rest, indicating that resting-state fMRI alone was an incomplete assay for stimulation effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental findings showing task-dependent modulation of stimulation effects.

claim: Resting-state fMRI alone was an incomplete assay for stimulation effects.
source: indicating that resting-state fMRI alone was an incomplete assay for stimulation effects.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the task-dependent nature of stimulation effects.

claim: The functional relevance of stimulation for memory performance was related to its effect on the task-dependent change in connectivity.
source: Furthermore, the functional relevance of stimulation for memory performance was related to its effect on the task-dependent change in connectivity, indicating that resting-state fMRI alone would not have identified functionally relevant effects of stimulation on connectivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation between task-dependent connectivity changes and memory improvement.

claim: Resting-state fMRI alone would not have identified functionally relevant effects of stimulation on connectivity.
source: indicating that resting-state fMRI alone would not have identified functionally relevant effects of stimulation on connectivity.
evidence: This claim is an inference about the limitations of resting-state fMRI based on the current findings.

claim: Individuals engage in a variety of uncontrolled and typically unmeasured cognitive operations during resting-state fMRI.
source: It is likely that individuals engage in a variety of uncontrolled and typically unmeasured cognitive operations during resting-state fMRI and that these at least partially drive resting-state fMRI connectivity outcomes (Van Calster et al., 2017; Chou et al., 2017; Kucyi et al., 2018; Hurlburt et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies examining cognitive processes during resting-state scanning.

claim: Uncontrolled cognitive operations at least partially drive resting-state fMRI connectivity outcomes.
source: and that these at least partially drive resting-state fMRI connectivity outcomes (Van Calster et al., 2017; Chou et al., 2017; Kucyi et al., 2018; Hurlburt et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing influence of cognitive processes on resting-state connectivity.

claim: The finding that stimulation effects on connectivity are particularly strong during a memory retrieval task is especially problematic for resting-state fMRI as an outcome for memory interventions given that subjects frequently and variably retrieve memories during resting-state fMRI.
source: Our finding that stimulation effects on connectivity are particularly strong during a memory retrieval task is especially problematic for resting-state fMRI as an outcome for memory interventions given that subjects frequently and variably retrieve memories during resting-state fMRI (Van Calster et al., 2017; Chou et al., 2017; Kucyi et al., 2018; Hurlburt et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is an inference about implications for resting-state fMRI methodology based on current findings and cited evidence.

claim: Subjects frequently and variably retrieve memories during resting-state fMRI.
source: given that subjects frequently and variably retrieve memories during resting-state fMRI (Van Calster et al., 2017; Chou et al., 2017; Kucyi et al., 2018; Hurlburt et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies documenting memory retrieval during resting-state scanning.

claim: Variable effects of stimulation on fMRI connectivity at rest would be expected based on the content and quality of memory retrieval subjects experience during scanning.
source: Variable effects of stimulation on fMRI connectivity at rest would therefore be expected based on the content and quality of memory retrieval subjects experience during scanning.
evidence: This claim is an inference about expected variability in resting-state outcomes based on uncontrolled cognitive processes.

claim: The current experiment accounted for challenges of resting-state fMRI by giving an explicit retrieval task during connectivity measurement.
source: The current experiment accounted for these challenges by giving an explicit retrieval task during connectivity measurement, which permitted differentiation of the PMN-targeted versus PFC-targeted stimulation conditions and identified functionally relevant effects of stimulation on task-dependent connectivity related to memory performance.
evidence: This claim describes the methodological approach used to address limitations of resting-state fMRI.

claim: The explicit retrieval task permitted differentiation of the PMN-targeted versus PFC-targeted stimulation conditions.
source: which permitted differentiation of the PMN-targeted versus PFC-targeted stimulation conditions
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental findings showing distinct effects for different stimulation conditions.

claim: The explicit retrieval task identified functionally relevant effects of stimulation on task-dependent connectivity related to memory performance.
source: and identified functionally relevant effects of stimulation on task-dependent connectivity related to memory performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation between task-dependent connectivity and memory improvement.

claim: The interpretation is limited without a different cognitive task control.
source: As our main comparison was between autobiographical memory retrieval and rest, our interpretation is limited without a different cognitive task control.
evidence: This claim acknowledges a limitation of the experimental design.

claim: It is possible that similar effects of stimulation on task-dependent connectivity could result using tasks other than those that involve memory.
source: It is therefore possible that similar effects of stimulation on task-dependent connectivity could result using tasks other than those that involve memory.
evidence: This claim is speculative, acknowledging alternative interpretations of the findings.

claim: Different cognitive demands have been strongly associated with connectivity of distinct functional networks.
source: However, different cognitive demands have been strongly associated with connectivity of distinct functional networks (Cole et al., 2014; Rissman et al., 2004; Mennes et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing task-specific network engagement.

claim: PMN connectivity is primarily associated with episodic and autobiographical memory.
source: with PMN connectivity primarily associated with episodic and autobiographical memory (Buckner et al., 2008; Svoboda et al., 2006; McCormick et al., 2015; Andrews-Hanna et al., 2014; Burianova et al., 2010; Daselaar et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies linking PMN connectivity with memory functions.

claim: It is reasonable to propose that task-dependent effects of stimulation on PMN connectivity would likely be specific for those that involve memory demands, including but not limited to autobiographical retrieval.
source: It is therefore reasonable to propose that task-dependent effects of stimulation on PMN connectivity would likely be specific for those that involve memory demands, including but not limited to autobiographical retrieval.
evidence: This claim is an inference about the specificity of stimulation effects based on known PMN functions.

claim: PMN-targeted stimulation increased PMN connectivity during retrieval more so than during rest, whereas PFC-targeted stimulation demonstrated the opposite pattern (rest > retrieval).
source: Notably, whereas PMN-targeted stimulation increased PMN connectivity during retrieval more so than during rest, PFC-targeted stimulation demonstrated the opposite pattern (rest > retrieval).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of connectivity patterns between stimulation conditions.

claim: The PMN but not the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex has generally been associated with vivid autobiographical memory retrieval.
source: Because the PMN but not the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex has generally been associated with vivid autobiographical memory retrieval (Svoboda et al., 2006; St Jacques et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies characterizing brain regions involved in autobiographical memory.

claim: The finding that PMN-targeted stimulation increased connectivity during retrieval while PFC-targeted stimulation showed the opposite pattern suggests that task-dependent connectivity increases occurred for the task that matched the function of the stimulated network.
source: this finding suggests that task-dependent connectivity increases occurred for the task that matched the function of the stimulated network.
evidence: This claim is an inference about the relationship between network function and stimulation effects.

claim: An area of dorsolateral prefrontal cortex was used as a control stimulation location as it is distinct from the PMN.
source: We used an area of dorsolateral prefrontal cortex as a control stimulation location as it is distinct from the PMN.
evidence: This claim describes the rationale for the control stimulation location.

claim: Counter to the effects of PMN-targeted stimulation, PFC-targeted stimulation caused nonsignificant reductions of PMN task-dependent connectivity.
source: Indeed, counter to the effects of PMN-targeted stimulation, PFC-targeted stimulation caused nonsignificant reductions of PMN task-dependent connectivity (Figure 2A)
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of effects between stimulation conditions shown in Figure 2A.

claim: PFC-targeted stimulation caused significant reductions of task-dependent connectivity in several distributed regions independent from the PMN.
source: and significant reductions of task-dependent connectivity in several distributed regions independent from the PMN (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of PFC-targeted stimulation effects shown in Figure 4B.

claim: These findings are consistent with previous reports showing reductions in task-evoked activity during memory encoding in prefrontal cortex due to the PFC-targeted stimulation protocol used here.
source: These findings are consistent with our previous report showing reductions in task-evoked activity during memory encoding in prefrontal cortex due to the PFC-targeted stimulation protocol used here (Kim et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim relates current findings to previous studies using the same stimulation protocol.

claim: Resting-state connectivity of dorsolateral prefrontal cortex with the hippocampus is not robust.
source: Although resting-state connectivity of dorsolateral prefrontal cortex with the hippocampus is not robust (Kahn et al., 2008; Yeo et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies characterizing connectivity patterns.

claim: Some analyses incorporating task-based connectivity have identified areas of dorsolateral prefrontal cortex that align with the ATN.
source: some analyses incorporating task-based connectivity have identified areas of dorsolateral prefrontal cortex that align with the ATN (Libby et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study identifying prefrontal regions associated with the ATN.

claim: The dorsolateral prefrontal areas that align with the ATN are distinct from the dorsolateral prefrontal location that was stimulated.
source: However, these areas are distinct from the dorsolateral prefrontal location that we stimulated
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of the stimulation location with previously identified ATN-associated regions.

claim: PFC-targeted stimulation caused no significant change in ATN task-dependent connectivity.
source: and, indeed, PFC-targeted stimulation caused no significant change in ATN task-dependent connectivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis showing no significant effects on ATN connectivity.

claim: PFC-targeted stimulation was a suitable control for PMN-targeted stimulation, based on a priori considerations and on the distinct pattern of findings.
source: Thus, PFC-targeted stimulation was a suitable control for PMN-targeted stimulation, based on a priori considerations and on the distinct pattern of findings that was identified for PFC-targeted stimulation versus PMN-targeted stimulation.
evidence: This claim is an inference about the validity of the control condition based on the experimental results.

claim: Although stimulation that influenced task-dependent PMN connectivity was delivered via lateral parietal cortex, the most robust effects on the PMN occurred in medial occipital-parietal and hippocampal portions of the PMN.
source: Although stimulation that influenced task-dependent PMN connectivity (PMN-targeted stimulation) was delivered via lateral parietal cortex, the most robust effects on the PMN occurred in medial occipital-parietal and hippocampal portions of the PMN.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of regional effects showing strongest changes in medial regions.

claim: The most robust effects on connectivity and memory-related activity due to lateral parietal stimulation occurred for the hippocampus and medial occipital-parietal regions rather than the stimulation site, consistent with previous findings.
source: This is consistent with our previous findings obtained with the current multi-day stimulation protocol, whereby the most robust effects on connectivity and memory-related activity due to lateral parietal stimulation occurred for the hippocampus and medial occipital-parietal regions rather than the stimulation site (Kim et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2014; Nilakantan et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim relates current findings to previous studies showing similar patterns of remote effects.

claim: Lateral parietal cortex provides anatomical projections to the mesial temporal lobe by which its stimulation can influence hippocampal activity.
source: One possibility is that although lateral parietal cortex provides anatomical projections to the mesial temporal lobe (Mesulam et al., 1977; Pandya and Seltzer, 1982) by which its stimulation can influence hippocampal activity
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies showing parietal-temporal connections.

claim: Lateral parietal cortex has relatively weak functional connectivity relative to medial occipital-parietal portions of the network.
source: it has relatively weak functional connectivity relative to medial occipital-parietal portions of the network (Kahn et al., 2008; Yeo et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies characterizing functional connectivity patterns.

claim: Lateral parietal cortex is less influenced by the influence of stimulation on hippocampal neuroplasticity because it has relatively weak functional connectivity.
source: and therefore is less influenced by the influence of stimulation on hippocampal neuroplasticity.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a mechanism for the observed pattern of effects.

claim: The degree to which a region's connectivity increases due to stimulation is predicted by its baseline connectivity with the hippocampus.
source: Indeed, we have previously found that the degree to which a region's connectivity increases due to stimulation is predicted by its baseline connectivity with the hippocampus (Wang et al., 2014), and this relationship has been replicated in an independent sample (Freedberg et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing this relationship.

claim: The effects of brain stimulation are locally disruptive at the stimulated location but can generate facilitation in connected regions.
source: An alternative possibility is that the effects of brain stimulation are locally disruptive at the stimulated location (Jacobs et al., 2016; Goyal et al., 2018; Kucewicz et al., 2018a; Mohan, 2019) but can generate facilitation in connected regions (Mohan, 2019; Ezzyat et al., 2018; Kucewicz et al., 2018b; Miller et al., 2015; Shirvalkar et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim presents an alternative hypothesis supported by citations to relevant studies.

claim: Like PMN-targeted stimulation, the effects of PFC-targeted stimulation on task-dependent connectivity also occurred for distributed regions other than the stimulated location, but without involvement of the hippocampus.
source: Indeed, like PMN-targeted stimulation, the effects of PFC-targeted stimulation on task-dependent connectivity also occurred for distributed regions other than the stimulated location (Figure 4B), but without involvement of the hippocampus.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of PFC-targeted stimulation effects shown in Figure 4B.

claim: PMN-targeted brain stimulation increases activity coupling among PMN regions when these regions are engaged by memory processing demands, rather than nonspecifically engaged during rest.
source: To summarize, our findings suggest that PMN-targeted brain stimulation increases activity coupling among PMN regions when these regions are engaged by memory processing demands, rather than nonspecifically engaged during rest.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main finding about task-dependent effects of stimulation.

claim: Task-dependent connectivity increases in the medial temporal lobe predicted improvement in a separate memory task.
source: Furthermore, task-dependent connectivity increases in the medial temporal lobe predicted improvement in a separate memory task.
evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis relating connectivity to memory performance.

claim: Memory enhancement by brain stimulation relies on dynamic (i.e., activity-dependent) rather than static changes in connectivity among select portions of the hippocampal-cortical network.
source: Thus, memory enhancement by brain stimulation relies on dynamic (i.e., activity-dependent) rather than static changes in connectivity among select portions of the hippocampal-cortical network, thereby reflecting a form of effective rather than functional connectivity (Friston, 2011).
evidence: This claim is an inference about the mechanism of memory enhancement based on the experimental findings.

claim: Memory enhancement by brain stimulation reflects a form of effective rather than functional connectivity.
source: thereby reflecting a form of effective rather than functional connectivity (Friston, 2011).
evidence: This claim is an inference about the nature of connectivity changes, supported by citation to a theoretical framework.

claim: The relationship between task-dependent connectivity and memory improvement was robust for the left hippocampus and surrounding medial temporal cortex.
source: The relationship between task-dependent connectivity and memory improvement was robust for the left hippocampus and surrounding medial temporal cortex, consistent with its established role in memory encoding and retrieval (Scoville and Milner, 1957; Squire, 1992; Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis and citations to foundational memory studies.

claim: The left hippocampus and surrounding medial temporal cortex have an established role in memory encoding and retrieval.
source: consistent with its established role in memory encoding and retrieval (Scoville and Milner, 1957; Squire, 1992; Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational studies of medial temporal lobe function.

claim: This finding is important given that nonspecific increases in connectivity could be detrimental to memory as well as other cognitive abilities.
source: This finding is important given that nonspecific increases in connectivity could be detrimental to memory as well as other cognitive abilities, as this would entail less-selective participation of the hippocampal-cortical network in memory (Shirvalkar et al., 2010; Froudist-Walsh et al., 2018; Henson et al., 2016; Warren et al., 2018; Gratton et al., 2016; Kim and Voss, 2019; Westphal et al., 2017; King et al., 2015; Geib et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is an inference about the importance of selective connectivity changes, supported by citations.

claim: Nonspecific increases in connectivity would entail less-selective participation of the hippocampal-cortical network in memory.
source: as this would entail less-selective participation of the hippocampal-cortical network in memory (Shirvalkar et al., 2010; Froudist-Walsh et al., 2018; Henson et al., 2016; Warren et al., 2018; Gratton et al., 2016; Kim and Voss, 2019; Westphal et al., 2017; King et al., 2015; Geib et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing the importance of selective network engagement.

claim: Stimulation-based interventions for memory disorders should strive to achieve memory task-dependent functional engagement.
source: Stimulation-based interventions for memory disorders should therefore strive to achieve memory task-dependent functional engagement, as identified here using PMN-targeted noninvasive stimulation.
evidence: This claim is a recommendation based on the experimental findings.
